title: Tornado in a Bottle: Spin a Vortex
description: Two bottles, a swirl of water, and a funnel cloud appears on command. Build a tornado in a bottle and learn why spinning water drains in a whirlpool spiral.

body.heading: A storm you can hold
paragraphs: Real tornadoes are dangerous giants of spinning air. Yours is a spinning funnel of water inside two bottles — small enough to hold, strong enough to show exactly how a vortex works. Every whirlpool, every draining bathtub, and every tornado obeys the same spinning rule.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The two bottles — one holds the water, the other catches it; they join neck to neck. The connector — strong tape (or a tornado-tube connector) sealing the necks together so nothing leaks. The water — filled with a pinch of glitter or a drop of colouring so you can SEE the spin. The vortex — the funnel itself: a hollow spinning cone of water with air at its heart.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: Two identical 1- or 2-litre plastic bottles, strong waterproof tape, water, a drop of dish soap (it makes the vortex last longer), and glitter or food colouring to make the spin visible. A grown-up does the joining.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Fill one bottle about two-thirds full of water. Add the drop of soap and the glitter. Swirl it once and watch the glitter drift — no funnel yet.
Step 2 — A grown-up joins the bottles neck to neck with layers of tape wrapped tightly round and round. Squeeze-test over the sink: no leaks allowed on this mission.
Step 3 — Flip the joined bottles so the full one is on top. At first the water just glugs down in gulps — air and water are fighting for the same narrow neck.

Step 4 — Now swirl. Hold the bottles and stir them in a quick circle a few times, then hold still. A funnel opens in the middle, the water spirals down smoothly, and the glitter races around the cone. That is your tornado — a vortex.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: Water draining straight down has a problem: air below needs to come UP through the same neck the water wants to go DOWN. Spinning solves it. The swirl throws the water outward against the bottle's walls, opening a hollow core in the middle — air rises through the core while water spirals down around it, both happy. Spinning water also speeds up as it nears the centre, like a skater pulling in their arms — which is why the funnel's tip is the fastest, wildest part, in bottles and in storms alike.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why does the water drain FASTER when it is spinning than when it just glugs?
2. Watch a bathtub or sink drain at home. Can you spot the same vortex? Which way does it spin?

takeaway: Swirling opens a hollow core in the water — air rises through the middle while water spirals down around it; that spinning funnel is a vortex, the same shape as a tornado.
supervision: A grown-up joins and seals the bottles and supervises; all flips happen over a sink, tray or outdoors.
safetyNotes: Plastic bottles only — never glass; a dropped glass bottle full of water breaks dangerously.
Check the seal over a sink before carrying the model anywhere: a leaking litre of water on floors is a slipping hazard, and wet floors get dried at once.
Glitter is a small-parts and eye irritant — a grown-up adds it, hands are washed after the build, and the tornado water is poured away by a grown-up, never drunk.
screenFreeExtension: Whirlpool watching: with a grown-up, stir a washing-up bowl of water with a spoon and race two floating leaf 'boats' — whose boat gets pulled into the vortex first?
